title: Psalm 117: All Nations, Praise the LORD
summary: In two verses, the shortest psalm in the Psalter calls every nation and people to praise the LORD. The reason it gives is Israel's own experience: his loving devotion toward his people is great, and his faithfulness endures forever.
story: Psalm 117 is the fifth psalm of the Egyptian Hallel (Psalms 113 to 118), placed between the personal thanksgiving of Psalm 116 and the great festal procession of Psalm 118. After a single person has told what God did for him, this psalm widens the circle as far as it can go, to all the nations. It captures in miniature one of the great threads of the Old Testament: God's choice of Israel was never meant to shut the world out. The promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3) stands behind a psalm in which the whole world is summoned to praise Israel's God for his love to Israel.
historical:
The psalm has no heading and gives no clue to its date. Its brevity has led some scholars to suggest it was a short doxology, a formula of praise, used to close or open a larger part of the Hallel; some Hebrew manuscripts even attach it to the end of Psalm 116 or the beginning of Psalm 118. Most traditions, however, count it as its own psalm. Like the rest of the Hallel it was sung at Passover and the other pilgrimage festivals.

The call to the nations would have had particular weight after the exile. Israel then lived among the nations, scattered through the Persian Empire and later the Greek kingdoms, and many Gentiles were drawn to its God. Books like Isaiah (for example Isaiah 56:6-7) speak of foreigners joining themselves to the LORD and of the temple as a house of prayer for all peoples. Psalm 117 gives voice to that hope in its simplest form.
cultural:
An ancient hymn normally had two parts: a call to praise and the reason for the praise, usually introduced by for. Psalm 117 is the purest example of that form, with nothing added. The surprising feature is the audience. National gods in the ancient Near East were generally worshiped by their own people; conquered nations might be made to honor the victor's god, but here the nations are invited to praise freely.

The reason given is striking too. The nations are to praise God not for what he has done for them but for his loving devotion “toward us,” that is, toward Israel. The idea is that God's faithfulness to one people shows the whole world what kind of God he is, and that watching him keep his promises to Israel is good news for everyone else.
literary: The psalm has the shape of a complete hymn in miniature. Verse 1 is the call to praise, in two parallel lines: praise the LORD, all nations; extol him, all peoples. Verse 2 gives the reason, also in two parallel lines, pairing God's loving devotion with his faithfulness, the two words that often appear together in the Old Testament to describe God's covenant character (as in Exodus 34:6). The closing Hallelujah forms a frame with the opening call. Its sixteen or so Hebrew words make it the shortest psalm and the shortest chapter in the Bible, but its reach is the widest of any psalm in the Hallel.

outline.t: All nations and peoples, praise the LORD
For his loving devotion and faithfulness endure

doctrines.note: The psalm calls all nations to worship Israel's God. God's covenant love for one people was always meant to become a blessing and a summons for the whole world.
Loving devotion and faithfulness are the two pillars of God's covenant character. The nations are invited to praise a God known for keeping his promises.
God's love is described as great, or mighty, and his faithfulness as enduring forever. These are not moods but settled qualities of who he is.

words.note: Goy, nation. The word often refers to peoples other than Israel, the Gentiles. The psalm addresses them directly, not as enemies to be conquered but as worshipers to be gathered.

Gavar, to be strong, to prevail. The BSB translates “great is His loving devotion,” but the verb suggests love that is mighty and overwhelming, prevailing over whatever stands against it. The same verb is used of floodwaters prevailing over the earth in Genesis 7.
Chesed, loving devotion, the steadfast and loyal love God pledges within his covenant. It is the love of a God who has bound himself to a people and will not let them go.
Emet, faithfulness or truth, from a root meaning to be firm or reliable. Paired with chesed, it says that God's love is not only warm but dependable, and the psalm says it endures forever.

christ: Paul quotes verse 1 in Romans 15:11, one of a chain of Old Testament texts he gathers to show that Christ came to confirm God's promises to Israel and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy (Romans 15:8-12). For Paul, the psalm is not a general hope but a promise being fulfilled in his own ministry, as Jews and Gentiles together praise God through Jesus. The faithfulness of the LORD that endures forever is shown supremely in the sending of the Messiah, who kept faith with Israel and opened the door to the nations.
questions: The nations are called to praise God for his love toward Israel. How can God's faithfulness to others become a reason for your own praise?
The psalm is only two verses long. What does it suggest about the value of short, simple praise in your prayer life?
Who are the peoples or groups you find hardest to imagine praising God alongside you, and what does this psalm say to that reluctance?
